t.3.3.1: Then Virādha, filling the forest with his voice, spoke again: 'Tell me, for I am asking you, who are you two, and where will you go?'
t.3.3.3: Know us two to be kṣatriyas, endowed with good conduct, dwelling in the forest. But we wish to know you: who are you that roam the Daṇḍaka forests?
t.3.3.2: Then Rāma, of exceedingly great splendor, told that rākṣasa with the blazing face, who was questioning him, of his own lineage, the family of Ikṣvāku.
t.3.3.4: Then Virādha said to Rāma, whose valour was true: "Come, I will tell you, O king; learn from me, O Rāghava."
t.3.3.5: I am, as is known, the son of Jaya, and my mother is Śatahradā; all the Rākṣasas on earth call me Virādha.
t.3.3.6: For through my austerity, by the grace of Brahmā, I have obtained invulnerability to weapons in the world, and indeed the state of being neither cut nor pierced.
t.3.3.8: Rāma, his eyes reddened with anger, replied thus to him, to Virādha, the rākṣasa of hideous form and wicked mind.
t.3.3.7: Leave this young woman behind and, without a thought for her, hurry back the way you came; then I will not take your lives.
t.3.3.9: Shame on you, vile wretch of base purpose! Surely you are seeking certain death, and you shall find it in battle. Stand still; you will not escape from me alive.
t.3.3.10: Then Rāma strung his bow, and swiftly fitting very sharp arrows to it, he struck down the rākṣasa.
t.3.3.11: With his bow strung with its bowstring, he loosed seven arrows, gold-feathered and of great speed, flying swift as Suparṇa and the wind.
t.3.3.13: Roaring a mighty roar and seizing a spear like Śakra's banner, he then shone forth like Antaka, Death himself, with his mouth gaping wide.
t.3.3.12: Those shafts, feathered with peacock plumes, pierced the body of Virādha and fell to the earth smeared with blood, resembling fire.
t.3.3.14: Rāma, the best of those who bear weapons, cut down with two arrows that spear, which was like a thunderbolt and blazed like fire in the sky.
t.3.3.15: Saumitri broke the left arm of that fierce one, while Rāma swiftly broke the right arm of that Rākṣasa.
t.3.3.16: With his arms broken, the terrified rākṣasa, resembling a cloud, swiftly fell to the earth like a mountain shattered by a thunderbolt. Then Virādha spoke these words to Kākutstha, the bull among men.
t.3.3.17: Kausalyā is blessed with a noble son, dear one! You are known to me as Rāma, and this is the greatly fortunate Vaidehī, and Lakṣmaṇa of great renown.
t.3.3.18: Because of a curse I entered this dreadful rākṣasa body; for I am a gandharva named Tumburu, cursed by Vaiśravaṇa.
t.3.3.19: And as I sought to appease him, that one of great fame said to me: "When Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, slays you in battle...
t.3.3.20: "Then, having regained your natural form, you will go to heaven." Thus spoke King Vaiśravaṇa to the one who was infatuated with Rambhā.
t.3.3.22: At a distance of a yojana and a half from here, dear child, dwells the righteous-souled and mighty Śarabhaṅga, a great sage radiant like the sun.
t.3.3.21: Not being attended upon by me, he grew enraged and spoke thus to me. By your grace I am freed from that most terrible curse; I shall go to my own abode. May good fortune be with you, O scorcher of foes.
t.3.3.24: This is the eternal law for rākṣasas whose life has departed: those who are laid in a pit attain the eternal worlds.
t.3.3.23: Go to him quickly; he will bring about your welfare. And, Rāma, having cast me into a pit, go on your way in safety.
t.3.3.25: Having spoken thus to Kākutstha, the mighty Virādha, tormented by the arrows, cast off his body and attained heaven.
t.3.3.26: Lifting up Virādha, the spike-eared one of mighty voice, who cried out with open throat and roared with a terrifying sound, he hurled him into the pit.
t.3.3.27: Then those two, bearing bows wrought brightly with gold, having slain the demon and taken Maithilī with them, roamed joyfully in the great forest, like the moon and the sun stationed in the sky.
